items.title: A.B. Spellman interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 19, 2022
items.q: you could drop in on people like Ornette Coleman or Alan Ginsburg or Larry Rivers, sit down and have a drink and watch them work and they’d talk to you.

ctx.x: I love the way you combine adjectives and nouns which — I’ll give you an example, at the end of “Dear John Coltrane” and you said, “If you, J.C. and Bach ever swap infinite fours” I just think that’s marvelous, like “infinite fours.” And it also begs the question how did you learn about the terminology that jazz musicians use all the time? The trading of fours, and the exchanges and back and forth? Was that by observing or did someone sort of take you under their wing and talk to you about that?

Well in New York I knew a lot of jazz musicians and I knew them very well. I mean that was a part of our world. The thing about the lower Manhattan arts scene in the 1960s was about as close as America ever got to say Montmartre at the turn of the 19th and 20th century, the modernism there. A great concentration of artists of all disciplines living in a relatively small area. They all knew each other, they all hung out together, they went to each other’s parties, they drank together, and the exchange was…

think was one of Ornette’s greatest, greatest tunes. You’d go by, I was roommates with a painter named Bob Thompson who is getting some attention right now, and Bob, he’s been dead for several years. And he’d be there working and he’d be there working and have his music on. That’s one, painters could listen to jazz and work. I always envied that. They’d have it up really, really loud and he’d be practically dancing into his canvas and he’d be talking about it. And it’s the same with all the musicians, I mean…
